title: Stop planner tools destroying and eliding state they report as intact
summary: Fix silent checklist destruction, a validation check that runs against rewritten content, and the prepare truncation that let a verified handoff ship incomplete.
description:
Current state:

Reported by a peer agent session working in /Users/antonio/projects/heca on 2026-09-15, after a phase handoff it had verified resume-ready turned out to be missing six facts a cold agent needed. Two live code defects, a wanted setting, a current design document, a binding pair previously conflated, and a confirmed by-design behaviour a future agent must not "fix" — all carried by the previous handoff precisely because no task holds them, all dropped by the new one. A human asking "are you sure it has full context?" is what caught it.

Every claim below was verified against the code in this repository before this phase was written. P103(F005) already fixed that session's payload-size complaints (handoff_show 59,823 -> 14,610 characters on heca P082) and the descriptionRef rejection (packages/plan-core/src/payload-fallback.ts now accepts three-segment paths). The defects here are the ones P103 did not touch.

Verified defects, worst first:

1. Replacing a task checklist silently destroys every tick and reports success. `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts:1614` does `task.checklist = checklist.map((item, index) => ({ ..., checked: false }))`, with `checked: false` hardcoded; `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts:1724` does the same. Nothing matches existing items by id or title, so editing eight titles loses all ticks and the call returns `updated: true`. The reporter lost six ticks and noticed only because an earlier agent had warned them in a handoff. A tool that reports success while destroying durable state is the most damaging defect in this set. Note the tool descriptions already steer agents toward `planner-task-checklist-toggle/add/remove` for granular edits, but the destructive path stays available and silent.

2. Supporting-document validation runs against content that auto-externalization has already rewritten. In `refreshPhaseHandoff` (`packages/plan-core/src/plan-store.ts:3770-3790`) an oversized body is externalized and `effectiveInput.content` is replaced with `externalized.content`. Validation then runs on that rewritten body (`:3795-3802`), and `validateHandoffContextSync` (`packages/plan-core/src/handoff-context.ts`) asserts `input.content.includes(requested.path)`. If the document path lived in the portion moved into the external file, the check fails against a body the path is no longer in, and `HANDOFF_SUPPORTING_DOCUMENT_INVALID` fires on a document that was correctly linked. The reporter's workaround — drop it from the manifest, leave it in prose — worked because the manifest is what triggers the check. Their guess about backticks in list items was wrong; the cause is ordering.

3. `handoff_prepare` returns the existing handoff elided, and asks the agent to reconcile against it. The protocol says "reconcile every still-relevant detail from an existing handoff", but prepare hands back a copy whose sections end in `[Extended detail continues in the linked planner document.]`, one of them cut mid-word ("⚠️ **Ownershi"). Prepare neither inlines the externalized text nor lists the headings it elided. The facts the reporter dropped lived entirely in that externalized document. This makes the loss structural, not careless.

4. `reconciledExistingHandoff` is an unchecked boolean. The author asserts it; nothing verifies it. The only gate on the most loss-prone step in the protocol is the agent's own say-so. Prepare knows the prior capsule's sections and could name the ones absent from the new content.

5. Auto-externalization splits without regard for structure. `externalizeOversizedHandoffContent` cut the reporter's body mid-numbered-list, moving "What is left" and half of two other sections out. A rewrite at 7,996 characters was kept whole, so the threshold behaviour is correct; only the split point is not section-aware.

6. Tool results are enormous even on success. A `planner-task-update` echo measured 122,628 characters in this session's own use and had to be spilled to a file by the harness. The reporter saw a rejected oversized description come back as a 125,115-character error — diagnosing a too-large payload cost more context than the payload did. The size limit is not stated up front and successful updates echo the entire task.

Goals:
- Make a checklist replacement preserve tick state, or refuse rather than destroy it silently.
- Validate supporting documents against the content the agent actually submitted, not a rewritten one.
- Give prepare's caller the previous capsule in full, or make what is missing explicit.
- Replace the unchecked reconciliation boolean with something the planner can verify.
- Split oversized handoffs at section boundaries.
- Bound tool results and state payload limits before a call fails.

Systems and files in scope:
- `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts` (task update at :1614, handoff tools, result shaping)
- `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts` (task update at :1724, handoff tools)
- `packages/plan-core/src/plan-store.ts` (`refreshPhaseHandoff`, `preparePhaseHandoff`)
- `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-context.ts` (`validateHandoffContextSync`, `externalizeOversizedHandoffContent`, `auditPhaseHandoff`)
- `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts` (the shared reply shaping added by P103(F005)/T408; new payload work belongs here, not in an adapter)
- `packages/plan-core/planner-skill.md` and generated plugin copies
- focused core, MCP, Pi and server regressions

Behaviors to preserve:
- The candidate-then-verify contract, persisted read-back hash verification, exact rollback, terminal-phase archive discovery.
- The 8,000-character capsule target and 24,000-character ceiling, and automatic externalization above the target.
- The payload reductions and the no-duplication invariant established by P103(F005), now pinned by `packages/plan-core/test/handoff-reply.test.mjs`.
- Harness-agnostic core per AGENTS.md rule 4: shaping and validation belong in plan-core, never duplicated per adapter.

Edge cases:
- A checklist replacement that renames an item — preservation by exact title match will not find it, so decide deliberately between id-based matching, positional matching, or refusing the destructive call.
- A supporting document whose path legitimately appears only in externalized text.
- A prior capsule so large that inlining it into prepare would breach the transport budget; the reporter's own phase is the realistic case.

acceptedDecisions.title: Checklist replacement carries ticks by title, then by position only when length is unchanged
acceptedDecisions.decision: `replaceChecklist(existing, titles, taskId)` in packages/plan-core/src/checklist.ts rebuilds a task's checklist from a plain title-string array in two ordered passes: (1) exact trimmed-title match, order-independent, each surviving existing item consumed at most once, so reordering and duplicate titles never multiply a tick; (2) positional fallback — carry the tick sitting at the same array index — but ONLY when the new list is exactly the same length as the old one, and only for a new title that had no exact-title match at all (an exact match's result, ticked or not, is never overwritten by position). Anything still unmatched starts unchecked; any previously-ticked item whose tick could not be carried is returned in `lostTicks`, and both adapters (plan-mcp and pi-adapter) surface a non-empty `lostTicks` in the tool result text and structured payload rather than reporting bare success.
acceptedDecisions.rationale: The prior behavior hardcoded `checked: false` on every checklist replacement, so renaming even one of several items silently destroyed every tick and still reported `updated: true`. Preserving by title alone fixes reordering but not renaming (a rename has no exact title to match). Positional fallback restricted to equal-length lists is what recovers a rename's tick without the failure mode of an unrestricted positional fallback: if list length changes, an insertion or deletion would shift every later item's position by one and hand its tick to the wrong neighbour. Restricting position-carry to "same length, no exact match" bounds the fallback to the one case it can resolve safely — a like-for-like rename — and leaves every other shape change (insert, delete, retitle-to-something-that-collides-with-another-existing-title) to fall out as an explicit, reported loss instead of a silent, wrong guess.
acceptedDecisions.implementationNotes: Both plan-mcp (planner-task-discuss at index.ts, planner-task-update at index.ts) and pi-adapter (task_update tool, and the interactive CLI `task discuss` handler) now call `replaceChecklist` instead of hand-building the array; grepped afterward to confirm no private copy of the checked:false mapping remains outside the two task-CREATION sites (plan-mcp/src/index.ts:1503, pi-adapter/src/index.ts:5043), where starting unchecked is correct because a new task has no prior state. Found and fixed a real bug in the first draft of `replaceChecklist` while writing edge-case tests: the positional-fallback pass used `carried[index]` (the matched item's checked value) as its own "was this title already matched" flag, so an exact match that correctly resolved to unchecked could be overwritten by position 2's stray tick. Fixed by tracking match-found separately from the matched value (`matchedByTitle` array). Regression: packages/plan-core/test/checklist-replace.test.mjs. plan-server's PUT /tasks/:id (serve.ts:1315) also has a `checklist` field but takes full ChecklistItem[] objects from the client rather than plain title strings — a different contract, out of scope for this decision.

acceptedDecisions.title: handoff_prepare inlines auto-externalized handoff content, budget permitting; names what does not fit
acceptedDecisions.decision:
Of the task's three options — inline the externalized text, return it as a separate field, or at minimum name what was elided — implemented the first with the second and third folded in as graceful degradation, not as separate modes.

`PlanStore.preparePhaseHandoff` (packages/plan-core/src/plan-store.ts) now reads back every document the *active* handoff's own auto-externalization produced (matched via the new `HANDOFF_AUTO_EXTERNALIZED_DOCUMENT_DESCRIPTION` constant / `isAutoExternalizedHandoffDocument` in handoff-context.ts — never a filesystem glob over `.planner/docs/`, only `phase.handoffAudit.supportingDocuments`, so a document superseded by an even later rewrite is not resurrected). Each is attached to the returned `PhaseHandoffAudit.externalizedHandoffDocuments[]` as raw content plus its `##`-heading table of contents (`extractHandoffSectionHeadings`), or `missing:true`/`content:null` when the file is gone.

`buildHandoffPrepareReply` (packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts) renders these in the `text` channel only (matching the existing-handoff precedent already in that file), sharing one `MAX_HANDOFF_CONTENT_CHARS` (24,000-char) budget across every document in order rather than bounding each independently — a document is inlined whole when it fits the remaining budget, truncated at a safe boundary when it partly fits, and named only (path, description, headings) once the shared budget is exhausted. `structured` carries only path/headings/contentLength/missing/inlined/truncated per document, never the body, so the existing no-duplication invariant (`handoff-reply.test.mjs`) holds unchanged.

Reused the existing 24,000-char ceiling instead of inventing a new budget constant: it is already the transport ceiling every other oversized handoff body in this file is bound to, so an agent only has to know one number, not two.
acceptedDecisions.rationale:
Budget is the real constraint. P103(F005) cut prepare from 64,560 to 18,033 characters on a 56-task phase; a naive full inline of every auto-externalized document (potentially unbounded — nothing caps the size of a submitted handoff body before externalization) would blow that back open and breach the pinned no-duplication/ceiling tests. Real data from the reporting phase itself (heca P082, read from disk, not executed against) shows why a per-document-independent bound is not enough either: that phase's active handoff carries two linked documents at once (one manual, one auto-externalized, 9,074 and 9,926 chars respectively) — the exact "several externalized documents from successive rewrites" edge case the task calls out. A shared budget bounds the worst case to one more ceiling's worth of text regardless of how many documents accumulate, while the realistic single-document case (8-11k chars, as measured on P082) is inlined whole and untruncated.

Choosing "inline, budget permitting" over "separate field" or "names only": a separate field pushes the decision of whether to read it onto the caller, and the task's own framing ("the elision must never again be invisible") is best served by content the agent sees without an extra round trip. "Names only" was rejected as the primary strategy because it reproduces exactly the original defect's shape at one remove — the agent is still told to reconcile against something it cannot see, only now the omission is at least visible. It survives here only as the degradation path when the shared budget is exhausted or the file is gone, which the task explicitly anticipated ("if your chosen option would blow the budget... that is itself an argument for a different option").

Filtering by `isAutoExternalizedHandoffDocument`'s description constant rather than by the `.planner/docs/handoff-p*` filename convention keeps detection decoupled from the naming scheme; filtering by the *current* `phase.handoffAudit.supportingDocuments` list rather than globbing the docs directory is what keeps this scoped to "still-relevant" content — a document abandoned by a subsequent rewrite the agent chose not to carry forward is deliberately out of scope, matching the protocol's own "reconcile every *still-relevant* detail."

Also fixed, in scope per the task: `externalizeOversizedHandoffContent`'s split point cut mid-word/mid-list-item because `boundedSection` sliced at a raw character offset. New `truncateAtSafeBoundary` (handoff-context.ts) retreats to the nearest paragraph, then line, then word boundary before the limit; `boundedSection` and `boundedHandoffForTransport` (handoff-reply.ts, the analogous raw-slice truncation used for the top-level persisted handoff and now reused for each externalized document) both call it, so the mid-word defect could not recur in one place while persisting in its sibling.

Verified by temporarily reverting both the plan-store.ts enrichment and the boundedSection safe-boundary call (raw slice restored) and confirming the three new regressions failed (43 pass / 3 fail) before restoring the fix (363/363 pass).

Measured on a bigPhase-style fixture (40 tasks) mirroring the P082 shape: prepare structured payload was unaffected in the no-prior-handoff case (unchanged from the existing ~size well under the 24,000 ceiling), and stayed under the same ceiling with three 24,000-char synthetic externalized documents attached (worst case exercised in the new "shares one budget" test). tasks.title: Stop a checklist replacement silently destroying every tick
tasks.description:
The most damaging defect in this phase: a tool reports success while destroying durable state.

Current state: `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts:1614` handles a task update carrying a `checklist` array with

    if (checklist !== undefined) task.checklist = checklist.map((item, index) => ({ id: createChecklistItemId(task.id, index + 1, item), number: index + 1, title: item, checked: false }));

`checked: false` is hardcoded and nothing matches against the existing items. `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts:1724` repeats the same construction independently, and `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts:1503` uses the same shape on creation (correct there, since a new task has no prior state). The call then returns `updated: true`.

Reported consequence: an agent in another project edited eight checklist titles through `planner-task-update` and lost all six ticks. It noticed only because a previous agent had written a warning into its handoff. Nothing in the result indicated loss.

Desired state: a checklist replacement never silently discards tick state. The input is a plain string array, so identity has to be reconstructed; decide deliberately between matching surviving items by exact title, matching positionally, or refusing the destructive call outright when it would clear ticks. Record the choice as a phase-owned Accepted Decision rather than leaving it implicit.

Implementation steps:
- Put the merge in plan-core, not in either adapter. Both adapters currently build this list themselves; after the fix neither should know how tick state is preserved. This is the same mistake P103(F005)/T408 corrected for reply shaping — see `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts` for the shape to follow.
- Apply it to both `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts` and `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts`, and grep afterwards to confirm neither kept a private copy.
- If the decision is to preserve by title, an item whose title changed is a new item and starts unchecked; say so in the tool description so the behaviour is discoverable before the call rather than after.
- If any tick would still be lost, the result must say which items lost state. A success result that silently drops ticks is the defect, so a partial-loss case must be visible in the response.
- Review the neighbouring tool descriptions: they already steer agents toward `planner-task-checklist-toggle/add/remove` for granular edits. That guidance is right but did not prevent this, because the destructive path stayed available and silent.

Behaviors to preserve: `createChecklistItemId` shape and stable ids; per-task C{n} numbering; creation at `:1503` starting unchecked; `planner-task-checklist-toggle/add/remove` semantics unchanged.

Edge cases: a replacement that reorders items; a replacement that renames one item and leaves seven identical; duplicate titles within one checklist; an empty replacement array (clearing the list deliberately); a replacement on a task that has no checklist yet.

Verification: focused `@agent-plan/core`, `@agent-plan/mcp` and `@agent-plan/pi-adapter` builds and their suites. Add regressions proving that editing titles preserves ticks, that a renamed item behaves as decided, that an intentional clear still works, and that any lost tick is reported rather than silent. Per AGENTS.md rule 17, no full repository gate.

tasks.title: Validate supporting documents against the submitted content, not the rewritten one
tasks.description:
A correctly linked supporting document is rejected because the check runs after the body was rewritten under it.

Current state: in `refreshPhaseHandoff` (`packages/plan-core/src/plan-store.ts:3770-3790`), a body above `TARGET_HANDOFF_CONTENT_CHARS` is passed to `externalizeOversizedHandoffContent`, and `effectiveInput` is rebuilt with `content: externalized.content` — the truncated remainder, with the moved text now living in a generated `.planner/docs/` file. This is why a verified resume-ready handoff shipped missing context a cold agent needed.

- Inline the externalized text alongside the persisted remainder, budget permitting.
- Return the externalized document's content as a separate field so the caller can read it deliberately.
- At minimum, list the headings and the `.planner/docs/` paths that were elided, so the omission is visible rather than silent.

tasks.title: Replace the unchecked reconciliation boolean with something the planner verifies
tasks.description:
The only gate on the most loss-prone step in the handoff protocol is the author's own say-so.

Current state: `handoff_write` takes `reconciledExistingHandoff` as a boolean. The agent asserts it; nothing checks it. `validateHandoffContextSync` in `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-context.ts` does not compare the new content against the prior capsule in any way. An agent that composed a fresh capsule and never looked at the previous one passes this gate exactly as easily as one that reconciled line by line.

Reported by a peer session on 2026-09-15, whose verified resume-ready handoff dropped six facts the previous one carried. They asserted `true` in good faith. Nothing caught it; a human did.

The planner is in a position to do better. `auditPhaseHandoff` already parses the prior capsule and, once P104(F005)/T415 lands, will have access to its externalized portion too. It can therefore see the prior capsule's sections and compare them with what the agent submitted.

Desired state: reconciliation is evidenced rather than asserted. When sections present in the prior capsule are absent from the new content, the planner names them and the author accounts for each — deliberately dropped, superseded, or folded in elsewhere. A bare boolean should no longer be sufficient on its own.

Implementation steps:
- Derive the prior capsule's section headings during prepare and carry them to write, keyed to the prepare token so the comparison is against what the author was actually shown.
- At write time, list prior sections with no counterpart in the new content and require an explicit per-section disposition before persisting.
- Prefer a typed no-mutation outcome that names the unaccounted sections over a generic refusal, in the style of the existing `HANDOFF_PREFLIGHT_REQUIRED` and `HANDOFF_REASON_REQUIRED` codes.
- Keep the cost of complying low. P103(F005)/T409 retains the submitted body against the prepare token, so a refusal here should let the author supply only the dispositions on retry, without resending the capsule. Verify that actually works rather than assuming it.
- Do not make this a completeness audit. P100(F021)/T396 deliberately removed the 16-section scaffold and the 14-category inventory because they made authoring verbose and failed late. This must stay a narrow check — which prior sections vanished — not a return to that contract.

Behaviors to preserve: free-form concise capsules with optional headings (P100(F021)/T396, second pass) — a capsule with no headings at all must still be writable, so the check must degrade gracefully when the prior capsule had no section structure either; the 8,000-character target; the candidate-then-verify contract; body retention from T409.

Edge cases: a prior capsule with no headings; a deliberate full rewrite where every prior section is genuinely obsolete; a phase whose prior handoff was archived rather than superseded; a first handoff with nothing to reconcile against; a prior section renamed rather than dropped.

Depends on P104(F005)/T415: comparing against an elided prior capsule would reproduce the original defect, since the sections most likely to be dropped are exactly the ones prepare currently hides.

Verification: focused core, MCP and Pi suites. Add regressions for a dropped section being named, a per-section disposition satisfying the gate, a heading-free prior capsule still being writable, and a refusal followed by a retry that supplies only dispositions. Per AGENTS.md rule 17, no full repository gate.

---
**Completion summary:**
Shipped: reconciliation is now evidenced, not asserted. New `validateHandoffSectionReconciliation` (packages/plan-core/src/handoff-context.ts) compares `##` heading text only — the full prior capsule's headings (compact capsule + T415's auto-externalized documents, read back fresh, never the elided copy) against the new submitted content's headings (submittedContent when auto-externalization ran, else content, so the planner's own compaction never causes a false positive). Any prior heading absent from the new content is named; the write is refused with a new typed HandoffContractError code HANDOFF_SECTION_RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED (details.unaccountedSections, details.recovery) unless the author supplies a substantive `sectionDispositions` entry per named section. No category list, no required prose beyond one short disposition line, no scaffold — this does not rebuild P099(F020)/T383's 16-section/14-category contract that P100(F021)/T396 removed.

Derivation: PlanStore.priorHandoffSectionHeadings(phase) (new private helper, packages/plan-core/src/plan-store.ts) computes the headings live from originalPhase at write time inside refreshPhaseHandoff, guarded by `phase.handoff.trim()` — not a separate cache keyed to the prepare token, because the existing handoffUpdatedAt optimistic-concurrency check already guarantees the live phase matches what prepare showed, AND because a handoff archived via handoff_clear between prepare and write leaves phase.handoff === "" while its stale handoffAudit.supportingDocuments still name the old externalized file — recomputing live (not from a captured snapshot) is what makes that case correctly require zero reconciliation instead of demanding dispositions for content that's already gone. preparePhaseHandoff exposes the same list as PhaseHandoffAudit.priorSectionHeadings (auditPhaseHandoff seeds it from the compact capsule; preparePhaseHandoff overlays externalized-document headings) so the agent sees the exact list to account for before drafting, not only as a late write-time failure — buildHandoffPrepareReply (handoff-reply.ts) adds one text line naming them when non-empty.

tasks.title: Bound tool results and state payload limits before a call fails
tasks.description:
Diagnosing an oversized payload currently costs more context than the payload did.

Current state, both measured rather than reported:
- A successful `planner-task-update` in this session returned a 122,628-character result. The harness had to spill it to a file and the caller then needed jq to read back whether `updated` was true. The tool echoes the entire task — full description, every checklist item, the whole statusLog — when one field changed.
- A peer session on 2026-09-15 had a `description` of roughly 17,000 characters rejected, and the rejection came back as a 125,115-character tool result. Roughly 13,500 characters were accepted on a later attempt, so a limit exists but is nowhere stated.

The result is a tool that punishes the caller twice: once for exceeding an undocumented limit, and again for finding out.

Desired state: a mutation result says what changed, not what the entity now contains in full. The size limit is discoverable before a call rather than after it fails.

- Shape mutation results in plan-core so both adapters inherit the bound. `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts` is the precedent from P103(F005)/T408: reply shaping lives in the core and both adapters render what it returns. Do not fix this in `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts` alone.

The existing `DESCRIPTION_MARKDOWN_FALLBACK_REQUIRED` path already tells callers to move long prose into `.planner/docs/` and pass a `descriptionRef`; that guidance should reach the caller in a few hundred characters, not a hundred thousand.

Verification: focused core, MCP, Pi and server suites. tasks.title: Stop the locate effect wiping the work-tree search box on every keystroke
tasks.description:
Reported by the user on 2026-09-15: after using the locate link in the active-tasks header, the Work Tree search box stops working — typed text will not delete, and even text that appears to be accepted never filters anything. Cause traced and confirmed in the code.

Current state:

The locate icon in the active-tasks header navigates to `/?locate=T00x` (`packages/plan-web-ui/src/components/layout/app-shell.tsx:51`). The Work Tree effect at `packages/plan-web-ui/src/components/dashboard/work-tree.tsx:247-306` then finds the task, clears the filters that could hide it, expands its feature and phase, scrolls the row into view, and calls `clearLocateParam()`.

`clearLocateParam` (`work-tree.tsx:26-30`) strips the param with `window.history.replaceState`. That is deliberate — the comment explains it avoids a router navigation so React Router's `<ScrollRestoration />` does not reset the page scroll after the row has been scrolled into view. But `replaceState` bypasses the router, so the `useSearchParams()` hook at `:243` never observes the param disappearing. `locateParam` and `locateNum` therefore stay set for as long as the component is mounted.

The effect's dependency array (`:297-306`) includes `tree.searchQuery`, `tree.hideDone` and `tree.onlyActiveBranches`, and the effect body clears all three at `:262-264`:

    if (tree.onlyActiveBranches) tree.setOnlyActiveBranches(false);
    if (tree.hideDone) tree.setHideDone(false);
    if (tree.searchQuery) tree.setSearchQuery("");

So every keystroke changes `tree.searchQuery`, which re-runs the effect, which clears it again. The search box is reset under the user on every change, for the rest of the visit. The same applies to the Hide Done and Only-active toggles. Nothing else sets `?locate=`, which is why the fault appears only after using that icon.

Those dependencies are not accidental: the effect is a deliberate retry loop that re-runs after expansion and filter renders until `document.getElementById('task-row-' + locateNum)` exists. The fix must keep that retry and stop the effect acting again once it has finished.

Desired state: one locate request performs its clear-expand-scroll-pulse once, and further renders leave the user's filters alone.

Implementation steps:
- Record the `locateNum` that has already been completed — a ref is enough, since it must not itself trigger a render — and return early when the current `locateNum` matches it. Set it at the point the row was found and scrolled (`:280-294`), alongside `clearLocateParam()`.
- Reset that record if `locateNum` changes, so locating a second task in the same visit still works.
- Leave `clearLocateParam`'s use of `replaceState` as it is; the scroll-restoration reason for it is sound. The defect is the effect trusting a param it knows the router will not see cleared, not the URL rewrite.

Behaviors to preserve: the retry-until-the-row-is-in-the-DOM loop, including the `phases.length === 0` early return at `:257` that keeps the param alive until data arrives; the smart tree-open mode switch; the manual scroll offset accounting for the sticky header and `.ap-search-sticky` bar; the 2500ms pulse and its cleanup; stripping the param without a router navigation.

Edge cases: locating a second task without leaving the page; a locate for a task that does not exist (the `!found` branch); a locate arriving before `phases` has loaded, which is the reason the retry exists; a user typing in the search box while the row is still being located.

Verification: focused Web UI tests in `packages/plan-web-ui`. Add a regression proving that after a completed locate the search query survives a change — the current code fails that. Per AGENTS.md rule 17, no full repository gate; project guidelines require a unit test for the component touched.

---
**Completion summary:**
The Work Tree filter bar survives a locate. Typing in the search box after using the locate icon now keeps what you type, deletes when you delete, and filters.

Cause and fix: `clearLocateParam` strips `?locate=` with `history.replaceState`, which the router never observes, so `locateNum` stayed set for the life of the mount. The locate effect lists the filter state in its dependency array — deliberately, as a retry loop waiting for the row to reach the DOM — and clears three filters in its body, so every later change re-ran the clear. Fixed with `handledLocateRef` in `packages/plan-web-ui/src/components/dashboard/work-tree.tsx`: the effect records the locate it has already carried out and returns early when asked to repeat it. The dependencies are untouched, as the task required — the ref ends the loop, not trimming them.

Keyed by `${location.key}:${locateNum}`, not by `locateNum` alone. A bare number would have broken locating the same task twice in one visit: the second click navigates to a URL the stale hook already reports, so the value never changes and the guard would swallow it. `useLocation().key` changes on every navigation, so a repeat locate runs. `locateToken` is in the dependency array for the same reason.

Behaviour decided with Antonio on 2026-09-21 and recorded on the task: locate still clears the filters once on arrival, so the row it jumps to cannot be hidden. What stops is the re-firing. After locating is done, a filter that hides the located row is honoured — locating is over, filtering has started.

Preserved: the retry-until-the-row-is-in-the-DOM loop, including the `phases.length === 0` early return that keeps the param alive until data arrives (that path deliberately does not mark the locate handled); the smart tree-open mode switch; the sticky-header scroll offset; the 2500ms pulse and its cleanup; `replaceState` without a router navigation.

Verification: `packages/plan-web-ui/test/work-tree-locate.test.tsx`, 4 tests — the filter bar surviving repeated changes, the one-time clear on arrival still happening, a second locate in the same visit working, and a locate not being consumed before the data arrives. Proven live: removing only the guard line fails 2 of the 4. Full web UI suite 105/105 across 15 files, `pnpm check` clean. Per AGENTS.md rule 17, no full repository gate at task level.

The tests drive the Hide done and Only active toggles rather than the search box. The search input is a third-party `elastic-input` contenteditable that jsdom cannot type into; all three filters are cleared by the same three lines under the same dependency loop, so a toggle that survives proves the query survives. This is stated in the test file header so nobody later mistakes it for an oversight.

Also removed, found while writing the test: the localStorage stub every Work Tree test needs was hand-copied into three test files, and this task would have made a fourth. It is now `stubLocalStorage()` in `packages/plan-web-ui/test/fixtures.tsx`, backed by a real in-memory map, and the three existing copies call it. Needed because this environment has no usable localStorage, so any component reading it throws on mount.

tasks.title: Bound the next-work recommendation and give it a command
tasks.description:
Asking the planner what to work on next costs about 49,000 characters to receive one task reference, and a human cannot ask at all.

Measured on this repository's own planner on 2026-09-15, via `recommendNextWork` with the exact inputs `planner-task-recommend` uses:

    current structured payload        48,869 chars
    the same answer minus `selection`  1,514 chars
    `selection` alone                 47,342 chars
      of which candidate.phase        40,765 chars
      candidate.task                   4,145 chars
      candidate.feature                2,296 chars

97% of the result is one field. `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts:1925-1937` builds a compact answer — `kind`, `taskId`, `phaseId`, `featureId`, `deviation`, `activeTask`, `nextFeature`, `nextPhase`, `nextTask`, `claims` — and then appends `selection`, whose `candidate.phase` is the entire phase object: every task's full description and completion summary, every checklist, every statusLog entry, and the whole persisted handoff body. `candidate.feature` carries the feature's complete `phaseIds` array. The no-candidate branch at `:1912-1922` does the same.

`packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts:5278` registers the `task_recommend` twin and has the same shape.

Nothing reads the fat. The compact fields already carry the answer, and `planner-task-recommend`'s own description says it returns "bounded typed claims" — the bound was never applied to `selection`.

Second, related gap: there is no interactive command for this. The Pi `/planner` subcommand list at `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts:255-290` covers task add/show/discuss/update/delete/start/complete and the three checklist paths, but has no `recommend`. `.planner/SKILL.md` states the omission deliberately — "Pause, switch, deviation, recommendation, requirement, and decision operations are available through the registered Pi tools below rather than every interactive `/planner` path" — so an agent can ask what is next and a person at the command line cannot. Pause, switch and deviation are arguably agent-only; "what should I work on next" is a supervisor question and is the odd one out.

Work:
- Stop sending `selection` whole. Keep `selection.kind`, `selection.reason` and `selection.deviation`, and replace `selection.candidate` with the composite refs and titles already computed for the text channel. Apply it to the candidate branch and the no-candidate branch.
- Do the same in the Pi twin. Shape the result in plan-core so both adapters inherit it, following `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts` — do not fix one adapter and leave the other.
- Add `/planner task recommend` to the Pi subcommand list and to the documented command paths in `packages/plan-core/planner-skill.md`, then regenerate the plugin copies with `pnpm plugins:sync` and verify with `pnpm plugins:check`. Its human output should be a few lines — the ref, the title, and the reason — not the structured payload.
- `planner-show` returns all ten project Accepted Decisions in full, with rationale and implementation notes, to list feature names. Check whether its callers need them; if not, bound it the same way.

## Folded in 2026-09-16: the third raw-slice truncation

`buildBoundedAcceptedDecisionContext` in `packages/plan-core/src/task-context.ts:76` truncates with a raw `full.slice(0, limit)`, so it cuts mid-word exactly as the handoff path did. It is the function behind the `planner-show` decisions payload already named above, which is why this lands here rather than in T417.

P104(F005)/T415 fixed the same defect twice over in the handoff path and left a reusable helper: `truncateAtSafeBoundary(value, maxChars)` in `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-context.ts`, which retreats to the nearest paragraph break, then line break, then word break before the limit. `boundedSection` and `boundedHandoffForTransport` both now share it rather than each carrying a copy of the bug.

Use that helper here too. If importing it from `handoff-context.ts` into `task-context.ts` creates an awkward dependency direction, move the helper to a neutral module both can import — but do not write a third implementation. Three independent raw slices in one codebase is how this defect survived; a fourth would be worse.

Behaviors to preserve: `kind`, `taskId`, `phaseId`, `featureId`, `activeTask`, `nextFeature`, `nextPhase`, `nextTask` and `claims` exactly as they are — the lifecycle protocol and the recommendation claims contract depend on them; the typed claim kinds including the `insufficient` handoff claim; the no-candidate branch's `activeTaskIds`; the rule that only a persisted resume-ready handoff is an actionable claim; `buildBoundedAcceptedDecisionContext`'s existing truncation notice and its `total`/`truncated`/`maxChars` reporting.

Edge cases: an active task present, so the recommendation is the active one; a recommendation with an approved deviation and a preserved resume target; the no-candidate branch; a phase whose handoff is large, which is what makes the current payload worst; an Accepted Decision context whose first decision alone exceeds the limit, where retreating to a boundary must still produce something rather than an empty string.

Related: P104(F005)/T417 covers oversized results for the mutation tools. This task covers the read/recommendation side, the missing command, and the Accepted Decision truncation; keep the two from duplicating each other's work.

Verification: focused core, MCP and Pi suites. Add a regression asserting the recommendation's structured payload stays under a stated ceiling for a phase with a large handoff and long task descriptions, and that every field the lifecycle depends on is still present. Add one proving `buildBoundedAcceptedDecisionContext` no longer cuts mid-word. Re-measure against the 48,869-character baseline above and record the new figure. tasks.title: Stop making the denial the documented path to starting a task
tasks.description:
Starting a task costs a guaranteed failed call, because the guidance tells agents to call first and learn the requirements from the rejection.

Current state: `packages/plan-core/planner-skill.md`, "Lifecycle-first context protocol", opens with "Before touching code, call `task_start` / `planner-task-start` ... The lifecycle tool may deny the transition and return typed diagnostics", and every numbered step that follows sits under the heading "When denied:". The documented happy path is therefore: call, get `CONTEXT_READ_REQUIRED` with `started: false`, perform the reads named in `nextActions`, retry. An agent following the skill exactly will always spend one wasted call per task start.

Observed this session starting P104(F005)/T413: the first `planner-task-start` returned `CONTEXT_READ_REQUIRED` naming the task and phase full views, both of which had to be read anyway before doing the work. Reading them first and then calling would have succeeded on the first attempt.

The gate itself is well built and should not change. It already reuses fresh attestations across sibling tasks — that same call asked only for the task and phase, not Project Guidelines or the feature, because those reads were still valid from earlier in the session. The defect is the ordering the guidance teaches, not the gating.

This is the same shape as P103(F005)/T407: a check that runs after the expensive step when it could run before it.

Work:
- Reorder the guidance in `packages/plan-core/planner-skill.md` so the normal path is: read the task full view and its phase full view (plus Project Guidelines and linked requirements when not already fresh in this session), then call `task_start`. Present the denial as the safety net it should be, not the expected first outcome. Keep every existing rule: reads may be completed in any order; only `started: true` proves work is active; a denial must never be converted into a status change to bypass the gate; a title-only summary never satisfies a read gate.
- Regenerate the plugin copies with `pnpm plugins:sync` and verify with `pnpm plugins:check`. The same text ships in `plugins/_shared/planner-skill.md.in` and `plugins/claude-code/skills/planner/SKILL.md`, and the project-local `.planner/SKILL.md` managed copy upgrades on planner load.
- Consider making the requirement discoverable without a failed call: have `planner-task-show` / `task_get` with `full=true` report the remaining gate state for that task — which reads this session has satisfied and which are still outstanding. An agent reading the task in order to start it would then already know. If this is added, it must be advisory only; `task_start` stays the sole authority on whether work may begin.
- Keep the typed denial codes and their `nextActions` exactly as they are. They remain correct and are the recovery path when an agent starts without reading, or when an attestation went stale mid-session.

Behaviors to preserve: every typed denial code (`PROJECT_GUIDELINES_READ_REQUIRED`, `CONTEXT_READ_REQUIRED`, `REQUIREMENTS_READ_REQUIRED`, `START_NOT_ALLOWED`, `ACTIVE_TASK_CONFLICT`, `TASK_DONE`); session attestation reuse across sibling tasks; the requirement that `requirement_list` be called with the exact `phaseRef` from `nextActions`; the phase work map delivered on a successful start.

Edge cases: an attestation that goes stale between the read and the start, which must still deny; a task started without any prior read, which must still deny and guide; `task_switch` when another task is active, which follows the same protocol.

Verification: focused core, MCP and Pi suites plus the plugin sync check. Add a regression proving a start succeeds on the first call when the task and phase full views were read first, so the reordered guidance is actually achievable rather than just better worded. Per AGENTS.md rule 17, no full repository gate.

tasks.description:
An agent reading a task in full cannot see where it sits in the order, so it cannot follow the ordering rule it has been given.

Its text summary carries title, composite ref, shortId, status and phase ref (`:1534`). Its structured payload carries exactly four fields (`:1561-1567`): `ref`, `description`, `descriptionRef`, `acceptedDecisions`. No priority, no dependencies, no sibling ordering. `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts` has the same shape in its `task_get` twin.

So the compact `planner-task-list` shows priority and the full detail view drops it: the summary knows more about ordering than the detail view does.

`planner-task-add` confirms creation ("✅ Task created: P104(F005)/T413 — … (planned)") without stating the priority it assigned. Eight tasks were created in this phase without a single priority number ever being shown.

`planner-task-recommend` does carry the ordering, but costs about 49,000 characters to deliver it (see P104(F005)/T419).

Consequence, observed in this session: an agent read P104(F005)/T415 and T416 through `planner-task-show`, formed its sense of what mattered from the prose, and proposed working out of order. The user caught it. `.planner/SKILL.md` already instructs "Follow the lowest visible ready priority", so the rule was present and the data was not — which is why adding more guidance text is not the fix.

Desired state: an agent deciding what to do next sees the ordering at the moment it decides, without calling a second tool or paying for the recommendation payload.

Work:
- Add priority to the full task view in both adapters — text summary and structured payload. Include the task's own priority and enough context to place it: the phase's ready task count and how many precede it, or the next-by-priority sibling ref. Keep it to a line; this is data, not a lecture.
- Add `dependsOn` to the same view. A task can be low priority and blocked, or high priority and ready, and neither is currently visible.
- Make `planner-task-add` state the priority it assigned, so the creator knows where the task landed.
- Have the planner-load recap name the recommended next task by ref. The recap already ends with a "Next step" line; naming the task there is data the reader can act on.
- Shape all of this in plan-core so both adapters render the same thing. Do not write the ordering line into `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts` and `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts` separately — see `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts` for the pattern this phase has used throughout.

The rule already exists in the skill and did not prevent the failure, because the rule was never what was missing. Adding guidance text would cost tokens on every call and leave the ordering just as invisible.

Behaviors to preserve: the compact (non-full) task view stays compact — it is the cheap identity read and must not grow; `markCanonicalFullReadForSessionId` must continue to receive the full rendered text so the read gate still attests correctly; the existing summary format and composite-ref conventions; `planner-task-list`'s current output, which is already correct.

Edge cases: a task with no explicit priority set; a phase where several tasks share a priority; a task whose dependencies are all done versus one still blocked; the first task in a phase; a done task, where ordering no longer matters and the line should not mislead.

tasks.title: Make an abandoned phase visible when work moves elsewhere
tasks.description:
Switching work to another phase silently leaves the previous one unfinished, and nothing surfaces it again.

Observed in this session, twice over. P102(F005) is priority 34 with three tasks; T403 and T404 were completed and T405 was left `planned`. Work then moved to P104(F005), priority 36, and ran through four of its tasks before the user noticed P102 was stranded. `planner-task-recommend` had named T405 with the reason "Continue the current phase before selecting new work elsewhere", but that output costs about 49,000 characters (see P104(F005)/T419) and nothing else mentioned it again.

Why the existing machinery did not help:

- `task_switch` / `planner-task-switch` atomically checkpoints the source task and preserves a LIFO return target. `task_deviation` / `planner-task-deviation` records a user-approved temporary detour with a resume target. Both protect an **in-flight task**.
- Nothing was in flight. T404 had completed, so there was no active task to checkpoint and no return target to preserve. What was abandoned was a **phase** with one task still planned.
- The phase simply stayed `in-progress`. `planner-show` reports feature-level counts and an authoritative active-task state, but never says "these phases are in-progress with work remaining, in priority order", so a stranded phase is invisible on the cheap read.

This is the same shape as the other defects in this phase: the data exists — phase status, phase priority, remaining task counts — but it is not present where the decision is made.

Desired state: an agent cannot start work in a lower-priority phase without being told that a higher-priority phase is still open, and a human reading the plan can see stranded phases without paying for the recommendation.

Work:
- On `task_start` / `planner-task-start`, when the target task's phase is not the highest-priority in-progress phase with ready work, return a non-blocking advisory naming the higher-priority phase, its ref, and its remaining ready task count. Do not block the start — the user is allowed to direct work anywhere; they must simply be told. Follow the shape of the project-context staleness advisory added by P102(F005)/T404: informational, attached to a successful start.
- Add in-progress phases with remaining work to `planner-show` and the planner-load recap, priority-ordered, with remaining ready task counts. Keep it bounded — a line per phase, not a phase dump, and mind P104(F005)/T419, which is bounding these payloads rather than growing them.
- Shape both in plan-core so the two adapters render the same thing; see `packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts` for the pattern used throughout this phase.
- Consider whether `task_deviation` should accept a phase-scoped target, so "we are deliberately leaving P102 to do P104" can be recorded with a resume target the way a task detour can. If it should, say so and scope it; if a phase-level advisory plus the recap listing is enough, record that judgement instead of building more machinery.

Explicitly NOT in scope: a guidance sentence telling agents to respect phase order. `.planner/SKILL.md` already says "Follow the lowest visible ready priority unless the automatic recommendation or an approved deviation says otherwise". That rule was present and was not what was missing — it failed twice in one session.

Behaviors to preserve: `task_start`'s existing blocking gates and typed denials, which must not be weakened by an advisory; the authoritative `activeTaskState` evidence contract in `planner-show`, which must keep proving absence from persisted task statuses rather than from counts; bounded human-facing output; the LIFO semantics of `task_switch` and the existing deviation records.

Edge cases: several in-progress phases at the same priority; a higher-priority phase whose remaining tasks are all blocked by dependencies, which is not a reason to advise switching to it; a phase in-progress because of an active task rather than an unstarted one; the first task started in a session, with no prior context; a phase left in-progress deliberately and indefinitely.

Verification: focused core, MCP and Pi suites. Add regressions proving the advisory appears when starting into a lower-priority phase, does not appear when the target phase is the highest-priority open one, never blocks a start, and that the recap lists stranded phases in priority order. Per AGENTS.md rule 17, no full repository gate.

tasks.title: Delete a feature the same way everywhere, and prove it happened
tasks.description:
Deleting a feature is written out four times, and two of the four leave broken phases behind. None of them checks the delete actually happened before reporting success.

The four copies:
- `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts:4238` — the `feature_delete` tool. When `cascade` is false it deletes the feature and **does nothing to its phases**. They keep pointing at a feature that no longer exists. It then reports `Feature deleted: ${params.featureId}` using the raw text the caller typed, and returns `details: { deleted: params.featureId }` — no read-back, no canonical ref, no count.
- `packages/plan-server/src/serve.ts:699` — `DELETE /features/:id`. Same orphan bug: filters the feature out, never touches phases. Returns `{ deleted: id }` without checking the id was ever present. Deleting a feature that does not exist returns success.
- `packages/plan-mcp/src/index.ts:1124` — the only correct one. Resolves the ref strictly, and unlinks phases when cascade is false, deletes them when true.
- `packages/pi-adapter/src/index.ts:1960` — the interactive `/planner feature delete` path. Also correct, but hand-written again.

This is the same shape as T413: a tool reports success while durable state is wrong. `planner-cleanup-orphan-phases` exists to clean up exactly the mess the two broken copies make — the cleanup tool is the symptom, not the fix.

Current state vs desired state: four hand-written deletes, two of them wrong, and a repair tool covering for them. Desired: one function in plan-core that all four call.

Steps:
1. Add `deleteFeatureCascade(store, featureId, { cascade })` to plan-core, next to the existing shaping helpers (`packages/plan-core/src/handoff-reply.ts` is the pattern for core-owns-it, adapters-consume-it). It resolves, deletes, unlinks or cascades the phases, reads back, and returns the canonical ref plus the phase count. It fails loudly if the feature was not there.
2. Replace all four call sites with it. Delete the hand-written bodies — do not leave one behind "just for the server".
3. Report the canonical `F00x` ref, never the caller's raw input.
4. Test: deleting with cascade false leaves phases alive and unlinked, not orphaned; deleting a missing feature fails instead of reporting success; all four surfaces produce the same result for the same input.

Edge cases: a feature with no phases; cascade true with phases that have their own handoffs (phase deletion already archives them — do not re-implement that); concurrent delete where the feature vanished between resolve and write.

tasks.title: Decide whether a resolved deviation still counts as open
tasks.description:
In `packages/plan-core/src/task-selection.ts:255`, `findResumeCandidate` builds its list of open deviations from four states:

```
.filter((deviation) => deviation.state === "approved"
  || deviation.state === "active"
  || deviation.state === "resume-required"
  || deviation.state === "resolved")
```

`resolved` means the deviation is finished. Calling a finished deviation "open" is at best confusing and may be wrong: the newest deviation wins (`newestFirst`, line 260), so a resolved deviation can outrank a genuinely open older one and drive the recommendation. Ten lines down, `returnIsRequired` (line 264) treats `resolved` as requiring a return, which is why it is in the list at all — but that is the only place it is needed, and pulling it into the "open" set to get there is what makes the filter misleading.

Background: a helper named `isPreservedResumeTarget` used to sit alongside this and filtered a different, broader state set than the live check. It was deleted as unused by commit 1bbccaf (T423). Deleting it removed the noise but not the question: is the surviving four-state filter right?

Current state vs desired state: one filter named `open` that includes a closed state, and a second condition that depends on that inclusion. Desired: the states are named for what they mean, and any list including `resolved` says why in the code.

Steps:
1. Work out whether a resolved deviation should be able to win `top` over an older approved or active one. Check the deviation tests in `packages/plan-core/test/` for the intended behaviour before changing anything — this is a read-first task.
2. If the current behaviour is intended, split it: build the genuinely-open set, and handle the resolved-needs-return case separately so no one reads `open` and gets it wrong.
3. If it is not intended, fix the ordering and add the test that was missing.
4. Either way, leave a test pinning what a resolved deviation does to the recommendation, so the next person does not have to redo this reasoning.

This is a correctness question, not a cleanup. It may end with no behaviour change and one test — that is a valid outcome, as long as it is written down.

tasks.title: Say that a task mentioned in conversation is not the next task
tasks.description:
Three Opus sessions across two projects have changed, or proposed changing, the task they were working on because another task came up in conversation. Each reasoned from what the human said instead of calling the recommendation tool, which would have told them to stay where they were.

Observed on 2026-09-22 in /Users/antonio/projects/heca: the agent had T474 in-progress in the planner and proposed a different task as "what's next", purely because the user described a capability in conversation and the agent went looking for the task that matched. It called neither `task_switch` nor `task_deviation`, and no planner tool ever named the task it proposed. A session in this repository reported the same failure about itself twice in the P104 work.

Where the planner already holds: if such an agent calls `task_start` on the second task while the first is in-progress, `ACTIVE_TASK_CONFLICT` fires and the transition is denied. The gate works at the action boundary. What it cannot gate is a sentence — an agent that merely proposes the wrong task in prose never touches a tool, so nothing intervenes.

Current state: `packages/plan-core/planner-skill.md`, section "References, discovery, and priority", says "Follow the lowest visible ready priority unless the automatic recommendation or an approved deviation says otherwise." That is correct and insufficient. It does not name the thing that actually displaces priority in practice, which is the conversation the agent is having.

Desired state: the skill states plainly that a task mentioned, described or implied in conversation is not an instruction to work on it; that the recommendation is what decides; and that a genuine change of direction is proposed explicitly with its reason, or recorded through `task_switch` / `task_deviation`, never assumed.

Why a rule is the right instrument here, given that P104(F005)/T421 rules reminders out of scope: T421's decision is that data an agent needs should be visible where the decision is made, rather than accompanied by a rule telling it to look. That applies to priority, which is a number the planner holds and can show. It does not apply here, because the planner cannot see the conversation. There is no datum to surface, so guidance is the only available mechanism. This is not a reminder to consult data — it is a statement about what does and does not constitute an instruction.

Implementation steps:
- Extend the numbered list under "References, discovery, and priority" in `packages/plan-core/planner-skill.md`. Keep it to two or three sentences: prose an agent skims must be short to be read.
- Do not add a reminder to any per-read or per-start surface. One statement, in the place the agent reads at load.
- Run `pnpm plugins:sync`, then `pnpm plugins:check`, so `plugins/_shared/planner-skill.md.in` and `plugins/claude-code/skills/planner/SKILL.md` stay in sync. The repository's own `.planner/SKILL.md` refreshes on the next planner load and is not hand-edited.
- `packages/plan-core/test/planner-skill.test.mjs` is the existing pin on this file's content; add the assertion there.

Edge cases: an agent legitimately told by the user to switch — that is an instruction, and the rule must not read as though a direct instruction requires a deviation ceremony before it can be followed. The distinction is between a task being discussed and a task being assigned.

Filed 2026-09-22 after Antonio observed the heca case and asked for the rule to live in the planner rather than in one agent's memory.

The canonical skill now says that a task discussed is not a task assigned.

The list below it was renumbered (old 4-6 became 5-7).

The edge case the task named is handled in the last sentence: "Being told directly to work on something is an instruction — follow it, and it needs no ceremony." tasks.description:
The guard that blocks editing when no task is in progress has three defects. Together they mean it obstructs the planner's own documented workflow, misses the way agents actually edit files, and gives the user no way to say yes.

Implementation is `guardPreToolUse` in `packages/agent-plan/src/index.ts:333-377`, invoked by `plugins/_shared/guard-pre-tool-use.sh.in` (and its derived copy) as a Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook.

**1. `.planner/` is not excluded, so the planner blocks its own protocol.**

`guardPreToolUse` checks only `tool_name` and never looks at the path, so an Edit or Write to anything under `.planner/` is refused exactly like a source file. The handoff protocol and the oversized-description fallback both instruct agents to create committed Markdown under `.planner/docs/` — `DESCRIPTION_MARKDOWN_FALLBACK_REQUIRED` literally says "create the suggested markdown file at .planner/docs/…". When no task is in progress, the planner tells the agent to write a file and then blocks it from writing it. Writing a handoff or recording task state must never be blocked: those are how an agent reports what it did, and they are most needed precisely when no task is running.

Fix: read the tool input's path (`tool_input.file_path`, and `notebook_path` for the notebook tool), resolve it, and return early — allow — for anything inside the planner root. Use the resolved planner root from `plannerRoot()`, not a string match on ".planner", so a path that merely contains the text elsewhere is not misjudged, and a symlinked or relative path still resolves correctly.

**2. Bash is exempt by design, and Bash is how agents edit.**

Line 344-346 deliberately skips every tool except Edit and Write: "Bash stays free so that git pull, build, test, ls, etc. always work." That reasoning is sound for read-only commands and wrong in practice. In a bypass-permissions session the harness instructs agents to make file changes with `sed`, heredocs and short scripts, so the ordinary editing path is completely unguarded. This was found on 2026-09-22 when the guard correctly blocked an `Edit` to `packages/plan-core/planner-skill.md` in this session, minutes after several source files had already been rewritten through `python3 - <<PY` without any challenge. The guard is not being circumvented deliberately; it simply does not see the edits.

Fix: inspect `tool_input.command` for write-shaped operations against paths outside the planner root — output redirection (`>`, `>>`, `tee`), in-place editors (`sed -i`, `perl -i`), file-creating copies and moves, and `rm`. Leave read-only commands alone: `git` (except commands that write files into the tree), build, test, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, `find` must stay free, and a false negative is much cheaper than a false positive here. Because the outcome is a prompt rather than a refusal (see 3), a heuristic that occasionally over-matches costs one question, not a failed operation. Keep the matching logic in one place so the Pi adapter's equivalent guard can use it rather than growing a second copy.

**3. It denies when it should ask.**

The hook returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` with a message telling the agent to ask the user to authorize a bypass. Nothing makes the agent ask, and the user is never shown a choice — the operation simply fails and the agent decides what to do next. Claude Code's `PreToolUse` contract supports `permissionDecision: "ask"`, which prompts the user directly.

Fix: return `"ask"` for edits outside the planner root, with a reason that states plainly what is happening — no task is in progress, this edit is to a file outside `.planner/`, and here is the task that would otherwise be started. Allowing it should behave like the existing bypass window so a run of related edits does not prompt on every file; `isGuardBypassed` and `planner-authorize-bypass` already provide that window, so reuse them rather than inventing a second mechanism. `"deny"` should remain only where it is genuinely correct, if anywhere.

**Behaviors to preserve:** no planner directory, no tasks at all, any task in-progress, or an authorized bypass all still allow immediately and cheaply — the guard runs on every tool call and must stay fast. The existing `startHint` naming a concrete task to start is good and should survive into the new reason text. The derived plugin copies must stay in sync: run `pnpm plugins:sync` then `pnpm plugins:check` after touching the `.in` file.

**Edge cases:** a path outside the repository entirely; a relative path; a Bash command touching both a planner and a non-planner path; a heredoc whose target is computed rather than literal (accept that this cannot be caught and do not pretend otherwise in the code comments); the notebook edit tool; a `git checkout`/`git apply` that rewrites tracked files.

**Verification:** unit tests over the decision function with fabricated PreToolUse events — planner path allowed, source path asks, in-progress task allows, bypass allows, read-only Bash allowed, write-shaped Bash asks. Keep the decision logic a pure function taking the parsed event so it can be tested without a hook harness; today it is welded to stdin and stdout.

Reported by Antonio on 2026-09-22: "MUST be fixed. but i don't want agent to be blocked for writing a handoff or updating a task. .planner should be excluded by this rule. and if the user allows skip this rule for code files too. so agent should ask if it can edit with no task in progress."

checklist.title: Extract the decision into a pure function over a parsed PreToolUse event
Never block any path inside the resolved planner root
Return ask, not deny, for edits outside it, reusing the existing bypass window
Detect write-shaped Bash commands; keep git, build, test and read-only commands free
Share the write-detection logic so the Pi guard does not grow a second copy
Unit tests: planner path, source path, in-progress, bypass, read-only bash, write bash
